[notes-n1] Notes 1. The frame under lateral load
Unit 5 ended with one force per floor on frame ABCD: the wind of Worked Example 5.1, from 11.63 kN at the roof to 18.75 kN at level 1. This Unit takes those forces down through the frame to the foundations, finds the moments they cause in every beam and column, and adds them to the moments of the vertical load.
[Figure: Figure 1. An unbraced frame under lateral load: every member bends in double curvature, with a point of contraflexure near its middle.]
Under horizontal forces at the floors, an unbraced frame sways. The floors move sideways almost as rigid bodies, and the rigid joints force each column and each beam to bend in double curvature : the moment at one end is opposite to the moment at the other (Figure 1). Somewhere in between the moment is zero, at a point of contraflexure . In a regular frame it lies close to the mid-height of every column and the mid-span of every beam.
A frame with rigid joints is highly indeterminate, and its exact moments come from a stiffness analysis, by computer. By hand, the points of contraflexure open a short cut: a hinge at each one removes an unknown moment. A frame of several bays is still indeterminate after that, and one more assumption about how each storey shares its load closes the problem. The two classic choices give the two methods of the course:
[Figure: Figure 2. The two assumptions: the portal method shares the storey shear by the spans; the cantilever method shares the axial forces by the distance from the centroid.]
Method Assumption added to the points of contraflexure Suits
Cantilever (§2, §3) the column axial forces are proportional to their distance from the centroid of the column areas, as in a cantilever bending as one piece tall, slender frames, where the frame bends like a cantilever
Portal (§4) the storey shear is shared between the bays in proportion to their spans, each bay's share split equally between its two columns low, wide frames, where the columns sway in shear
Quick check (not graded): In a regular unbraced frame under wind, where are the bending moments of a column of an intermediate storey taken as zero?
Options: At both ends | At mid-height | At the floor below | Nowhere: the moment is constant
Explanation shown after answering: The column bends in double curvature, so its end moments are opposite and the moment passes through zero near mid-height. Both methods put a hinge there, and at the mid-span of the beams.
Key points:
- Under lateral load every member of an unbraced frame bends in double curvature; its moment is zero near mid-height or mid-span.
- Hinges at the points of contraflexure, plus one assumption per storey, make each storey statically determinate.
- Cantilever method: axial forces by the distance from the centroid. Portal method: the storey shear by the spans.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. The cantilever method
Cantilever method: the assumptions (1) The points of contraflexure are at the mid-height of every column and the mid-span of every beam. (2) The axial force in each column is proportional to its distance from the centroid of the column areas; with equal areas, the centroid is the average position of the columns. The windward columns are in tension, the leeward ones in compression (course notes; Mosley, Bungey and Hulse §3.4.2).
Cut the frame at the mid-height of the columns of a storey, where their moments are zero. The part above the cut carries the lateral loads above it, and its overturning moment about the cut is resisted by the axial forces of the columns alone:
EQUATION (6.1): M_o = \sum_{k \,\text{above}} F_k\,\left(z_k - z_{cut}\right), \qquad z_{cut} = \text{mid-height of the storey}
EQUATION (6.2): N_i = r_i\,P, \qquad r_i = \frac{d_i}{d_{min}}, \qquad P = \frac{M_o}{\sum \lvert r_i \rvert\,\lvert d_i \rvert}
Here d_i is the distance of column i from the centroid and P the axial force of a column at the smallest distance d_{min}. Frame ABCD has columns at 0, 6, 12 and 18 m: the centroid is at 9 m, the distances 9, 3, 3 and 9 m, so the axial forces are 3P, P, P and 3P, and Σ|r||d| = 3 × 9 + 3 + 3 + 3 × 9 = 60 m.
[Figure: Figure 3. Storey 1 of Worked Example 6.1, cut at the column mid-heights: M_o = 13.96 × 1.75 kN m gives the axial forces; the beam cuts give the column shears.]
Beam shears. Cut each beam at mid-span as well. The part of the storey to the left of a beam cut is in vertical equilibrium: the shear in the beam at the cut balances the changes of axial force of the columns to its left, ΔN_i = N_i − N_{i,storey above}:
EQUATION (6.3): F_j = \sum_{i \le j} \Delta N_i \qquad \text{(the beam to the right of column } j\text{, at the level above the storey)}
Column shears. Take moments about each beam cut for the same part: the column shears of the storey, acting at h/2 below the beam, and those of the storey above, at h/2 above it, balance the moments of the ΔN_i. Working from the windward column gives each column shear in turn; the last one follows from ΣH = the storey shear. The moments are then the shears times half the length:
EQUATION (6.4): M_{col} = H\,\frac{h}{2} \;\;\text{(top and bottom of the storey)}, \qquad M_{beam} = F\,\frac{L}{2} \;\;\text{(both ends of the beam)}
Quick check (not graded): A frame has three columns of equal area at 0, 6 and 10 m. Which axial-force ratios does the cantilever method give?
Options: 1 : 1 : 1 | 1 : 0 : 1 | 8 : 1 : 7 | 6 : 0 : 4
Explanation shown after answering: The centroid is at (0 + 6 + 10)/3 = 5.33 m; the distances are 5.33, 0.67 and 4.67 m, and divided by the smallest, 0.67 m, they give 8 : 1 : 7. The middle column is not at the centroid, so it takes a small axial force, on the leeward side.
Quick check (not graded): In storey 1 of frame ABCD, M_o = 24.42 kN m and Σ|r||d| = 60 m. What is the axial force in column A?
Options: 1.22 kN, tension | 0.41 kN, tension | 1.22 kN, compression | 4.07 kN, tension
Explanation shown after answering: P = 24.42/60 = 0.407 kN, and A, the windward outer column, takes 3P = 1.22 kN in tension. D takes the same in compression.
Key points:
- Cut at the column mid-heights: the overturning moment of the loads above is resisted by the column axial forces, in proportion to their distance from the centroid.
- Beam shears from vertical equilibrium of the part left of each beam cut; column shears from moments about each beam cut; the last from ΣH.
- Moments: H h/2 in the columns, F L/2 in the beams.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. Storey by storey: the course frame
Worked Example 6.1 (Examples tab) analyses frame ABCD of the course notes under the wind of Worked Example 5.1 with the design factor of the course method, W_d = 1.2W_k: 13.96 kN at the roof to 22.50 kN at level 1, 160.63 kN in all. The table gives every storey; by symmetry C and D mirror B and A, with the axial forces in compression.
Storey M_o (kN m) P (kN) N_A / N_B (kN) H_A / H_B (kN) M_{col} A / B (kN m) M_{beam} AB / BC (kN m)
1 (Roof–Level 6) 24.42 0.407 1.22 / 0.41 2.09 / 4.88 3.66 / 8.55 3.66 / 4.88
2 (Level 6–Level 5) 120.82 2.014 6.04 / 2.01 6.17 / 14.40 10.80 / 25.19 14.46 / 19.28
3 (Level 5–Level 4) 310.61 5.177 15.53 / 5.18 10.10 / 23.56 17.67 / 41.23 28.47 / 37.96
4 (Level 4–Level 3) 589.97 9.833 29.50 / 9.83 13.85 / 32.31 24.23 / 56.54 41.90 / 55.87
5 (Level 3–Level 2) 954.51 15.909 47.73 / 15.91 17.40 / 40.60 30.45 / 71.05 54.68 / 72.91
6 (Level 2–Level 1) 1399.21 23.320 69.96 / 23.32 20.72 / 48.34 36.26 / 84.60 66.71 / 88.94
7 (Level 1–Ground) 1962.18 32.703 98.11 / 32.70 24.09 / 56.22 48.19 / 112.44 84.44 / 112.59
Three things grow down the frame. The overturning moment grows fastest, with the force and the lever arm together, and with it the axial forces: 98.1 kN in each outer column of the ground storey. The storey shear grows with the sum of the forces, and with it the column shears and moments. The interior columns take about 2.3 times the shear of the outer ones, and the middle beam carries the largest moments, 112.59 kN m at level 1.
Check every joint. At a joint the beam moments must balance the column moments. At B on level 1 the beams give 84.44 + 112.59 = 197.04 kN m and the columns 84.60 (above) + 112.44 (below) = 197.04 kN m. A storey that fails this check, or whose column shears do not add up to the storey shear, has a slip in it.
Against the notes. The course notes’ Example 6 runs the same method with the forces of the wind of the 18 m face (11.3 kN at the roof to 16.7 kN at level 1). With those forces the method gives P = 0.330, 1.625 and 4.162 kN in the top three storeys, as the notes print (0.33, 1.62 and 4.16), and column shears equal to theirs within rounding. With the wind in the plane of the frame (Unit 5, decision D57) every force is about 28 % larger, and so is every result: the ground-storey interior column moment is 112.44 kN m against 87.75 kN m with the notes’ wind.
Quick check (not graded): At an interior joint of level 1 of frame ABCD, the column above takes 84.60 kN m and the column below 112.44 kN m. The beam on the left takes 84.44 kN m. What must the beam on the right take?
Options: 84.44 kN m | 28.00 kN m | 197.04 kN m | 112.60 kN m
Explanation shown after answering: The joint is in equilibrium: the beams together balance the columns together, 84.60 + 112.44 = 197.04 kN m, so the right beam takes 197.04 − 84.44 = 112.60 kN m (the table: 112.59, the difference is rounding).
Key points:
- The overturning moment, the axial forces and the shears all grow down the frame; the ground storey and level 1 govern.
- Check each storey: ΣH = the storey shear, and at every joint Σ beam moments = Σ column moments.
- With the wind of D57 every result of the notes’ Example 6 is about 28 % larger.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. The portal method
Portal method: the assumptions (1) The points of contraflexure are at the mid-height of every column and the mid-span of every beam. (2) The shear of each storey is shared between the bays in proportion to their spans. (3) The shear of each bay is shared equally by its two columns, so an interior column takes half of each bay beside it (course notes; Mosley, Bungey and Hulse §3.4.2).
EQUATION (6.5): H_i = k_i\,V, \qquad k_i = \frac{L_{left} + L_{right}}{2\sum L}, \qquad V = \sum_{\text{above}} F
The column moments follow at once, H h/2 at the top and bottom of the storey. The beam moments come from the equilibrium of each joint, working from the windward side: the beam on the right of a joint balances the columns above and below it, less the beam on its left. The beam shear follows from the moment zero at mid-span, and each beam shear passes to the columns as axial force:
EQUATION (6.6): M_{b,right} = M_{c,above} + M_{c,below} - M_{b,left}, \qquad F = \frac{2M_b}{L}, \qquad \Delta N_i = F_{left} - F_{right}
[Figure: Figure 4. The portal method at the roof of Faded Example 6.2: the joint balance from A to D gives the beam moments, and every beam carries the same shear.]
Two results are worth knowing. Because every column takes the half spans beside it, every beam at a level carries the same shear : at the roof of Faded Example 6.2, F = 0.62 kN in all three beams, although their spans are 6, 5 and 8 m. So the interior columns receive equal and opposite beam shears and only the two outer columns carry axial force from the wind. The joint balance also closes by itself at the leeward column: the last beam moment equals the column moments there, a free check of the arithmetic.
[Figure: Figure 5. The same storey by the two assumptions (Activity 6A): close for the columns, further apart for the beams.]
Portal or cantilever? On frame ABCD the two methods give column moments within about 10 % (Figure 5): 53.54 against 48.19 kN m in an outer column of the ground storey, 107.08 against 112.44 in an interior one. The beams differ more: the portal method gives every beam of level 1 the same 93.83 kN m, the cantilever method 84.44 in the outer beams and 112.59 in the middle one, 20 % more. Neither is exact. The portal method suits low, wide frames whose columns sway in shear; the cantilever method suits tall, slender frames that bend as a whole. The course notes use the cantilever method for the seven-storey frame (Example 6).
Quick check (not graded): A storey with spans 6, 5 and 8 m carries a storey shear of 19.25 kN. By the portal method, what shear does column B (between the 6 m and 5 m spans) take?
Options: 4.81 kN | 5.57 kN | 6.42 kN | 3.04 kN
Explanation shown after answering: k_B = (6 + 5)/(2 × 19) = 0.289, so H_B = 0.289 × 19.25 = 5.57 kN. An equal share would be 19.25/4 = 4.81 kN; 3.04 kN is column A’s share, (0 + 6)/38.
Quick check (not graded): By the portal method, which columns of a three-bay frame carry axial force from the wind?
Options: All four, in proportion to their distance from the centroid | The two interior ones only | The two outer ones only | None
Explanation shown after answering: Every beam at a level carries the same shear, so an interior column receives equal and opposite shears from its two beams: no axial force. The outer columns take the beam shears down, tension on the windward side and compression on the leeward side. A is the cantilever method’s assumption.
Key points:
- Portal: the storey shear by k_i = (L_{left} + L_{right})/(2ΣL); the beam moments joint by joint from the windward side.
- Every beam at a level carries the same shear; only the outer columns take axial force.
- The two methods agree closely for the columns of a regular frame, less for the beams; portal for low frames, cantilever for tall ones.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. Adding the wind to the vertical load
The course method takes the wind with the vertical load by BS 8110 load combination 3, 1.2G_k + 1.2Q_k + 1.2W_k, with every span loaded, as the course notes’ Example 7 does. It is a course convention, not an EN 1990 combination (§6). BS 8110 also asks for 1.4G_k + 1.6Q_k (the analyses of Units 3 and 4) and for 1.0G_k or 1.4G_k with 1.4W_k, which the notes do not take.
At one level, the combination has three parts. (1) The vertical load: the one-level sub-frame of Unit 4 with every span at 1.2(G_k + Q_k) gives the beam-end, span and column moments. (2) The wind: the lateral analysis with W_d = 1.2W_k gives the beam moments of the level (from the storey below it), the upper column moments (from the storey above) and the lower column moments (from the storey below). (3) The sum, by superposition, for both wind directions:
[Figure: Figure 6. The wind hogs one end of a beam and relieves the other; the vertical load hogs both. Wind from the other side: the mirror image.]
EQUATION (6.7): M_{end} = M_v + M_w \;\text{(hogging)}, \qquad M_{rev} = M_w - M_v \;\text{(sagging, if positive)}, \qquad M_{col} = \lvert M_v \rvert + M_w
The span moment is the largest value of M_v(x) ± M_w(1 − 2x/L) along the span: the wind moment varies linearly from one end to the other, so the largest sagging moves towards the relieved end and grows. For frame ABCD at level 1 (Activity 6B):
Span M_v left M_v right M_w Combined left Combined right Span sagging Reversal
AB 82.17 165.61 84.44 166.61 250.05 113.61 2.28 at A
BC 146.91 146.91 112.59 259.51 259.51 75.92 —
CD 165.61 82.17 84.44 250.05 166.61 113.61 2.28 at D
Joint Upper: M_v + M_w = Lower: M_v + M_w =
A 43.82 36.26 80.08 38.34 48.19 86.53
B 9.97 84.60 94.57 8.72 112.44 121.16
[Figure: Figure 7. The combination at level 1 of frame ABCD, BS 8110 combination 3 (kN m).]
The wind adds most where the vertical load gives least. The hogging of BC at B rises from 146.91 to 259.51 kN m (+77 %), but the lower column at B, which the balanced vertical load hardly bends (8.72 kN m), takes 121.16 kN m, fourteen times as much. At A the wind moment 84.44 kN m exceeds the vertical 82.17 kN m, so with the wind from the left the end reverses : a sagging moment of 2.28 kN m that needs bottom bars anchored at the support. With the wind of the notes (the 18 m face) the same values are 235.07 and 96.47 kN m.
Quick check (not graded): At an end support the vertical load gives 60 kN m of hogging and the wind 75 kN m. What does the course method design that end for?
Options: 135 kN m hogging only | 15 kN m hogging only | 75 kN m hogging only | 135 kN m hogging, and 15 kN m sagging for the other wind direction
Explanation shown after answering: With the wind one way the end hogs by 60 + 75 = 135 kN m; with the wind the other way it is relieved, 60 − 75 = −15: a sagging of 15 kN m. Both go into the design: top bars for 135, bottom bars anchored at the support for 15.
Key points:
- Course method: 1.2(G_k + Q_k) on every span with 1.2W_k (BS 8110 combination 3), by superposition at each level.
- Beam ends: M_v + M_w for the hogging, M_w − M_v for a reversal; columns: |M_v| + M_w.
- The wind matters most where the vertical load is balanced: the interior columns and the end supports.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. The EN 1990 route, and which method when
The code route is EN 1990 Eq. 6.10 with the Malaysian National Annex, the default of the RC Design app. The wind is a variable action like the imposed load, and each in turn leads, with the other at its combination value (ψ_0 = 0.7 for the imposed load and 0.5 for the wind, as the app takes them):
Combination (EN 1990 Eq. 6.10) Factors What it checks
1 Imposed load leading 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k + 0.75W_k the largest vertical load with some wind
2 Wind leading 1.35G_k + 1.05Q_k + 1.5W_k the largest wind moments: the columns and the hogging at the ends
3 Permanent favourable 1.0G_k + 1.5W_k the reversal of a beam end, with the least vertical load
On this route the app also adds the EC2 geometric imperfections (5.2; decision D83): at each floor H_i = θ_iN_i, with θ_i = 1/379.5 for the course frame and N_i the factored vertical load that the floor brings in, about 3.5 kN per level beside the wind. On the workbook’s frame (app case FA9, spans 6, 5 and 8 m) combination 2 governs the hogging (430.4 kN m at C) and every column (the lower column at C, 211.6 kN m), and combination 3 gives a reversal of up to 79.2 kN m at a relieved beam end. The course method finds 2.28 kN m at A of frame ABCD: a different frame, but the trend is general, since 1.0G_k is much less than 1.2(G_k + Q_k) and 1.5W_k more than 1.2W_k.
Which method, and how far to trust it. Both approximate methods assume a regular frame: equal storey heights within a storey, columns of equal area (cantilever), points of contraflexure at the middle. They ignore the relative stiffness of the beams and the columns, which decides where the points of contraflexure really are; in the ground storey of a frame with fixed bases the point moves up, and a stiff beam over flexible columns changes the shares. The course uses them to understand the load path and to check a computer analysis by its order of magnitude and its equilibrium; the design values of a real frame come from a stiffness analysis.
Quick check (not graded): Which EN 1990 combination checks whether a beam end reverses under the wind?
Options: 1.35G_k + 1.5Q_k + 0.75W_k | 1.35G_k + 1.05Q_k + 1.5W_k | 1.0G_k + 1.5W_k | 1.2G_k + 1.2Q_k + 1.2W_k
Explanation shown after answering: A reversal needs a small vertical moment and a large wind moment: the permanent load at its favourable value 1.0 with the wind leading. D is the course method (BS 8110), which keeps the imposed load on every span and so finds a much smaller reversal.
Key points:
- EN 1990: imposed leading, wind leading, and 1.0G_k + 1.5W_k for the reversal; the app adds the EC2 imperfections (D83).
- The course method stays BS 8110 combination 3; the EN 1990 route gives larger wind moments and larger reversals.
- Approximate methods explain the load path and check a computer analysis; they are not the final design values.

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions
Exam type short written answers Time ≈ 3 min each
Questions
- Why may the points of contraflexure be taken at mid-height and mid-span, and where is that poorest?
- Why does the portal method give every beam at a level the same shear?
- In frame ABCD at level 1 the wind adds 77 % to the hogging of BC at B but makes the lower column at B fourteen times larger. Why the difference?
- What is the reversal of a beam end, and what does it need in the design?
Write your four answers first, then open the model answers one by one.
## Answer 1 Double curvature, if the members are alike
With rigid joints and floors moving sideways, each column and beam bends in double curvature; when the beams and columns at both ends of a member are alike, its end moments are nearly equal and opposite, so the zero falls near the middle. It is poorest in the ground storey with fixed bases, where the point moves up from mid-height, and wherever a stiff member meets a flexible one.
## Answer 2 The shares are half spans
Each column takes the half spans beside it, so the joint balance gives each beam a moment proportional to its span: M_b = (V_{above}h_{above} + V h)L/(4ΣL). Then F = 2M_b/L is the same for every span, and an interior column receives equal and opposite shears from its two beams: no axial force.
## Answer 3 Balanced against antisymmetric
Under the vertical load the beams on both sides of B hog almost equally, so the joint is nearly balanced and the columns take only the small difference, 8.72 kN m below B. The wind bends the frame antisymmetrically: every beam end and every column at the joint turns the same way, and the column takes its full share, 112.44 kN m. The hogging was large already (146.91 kN m), so the same wind adds less in proportion.
## Answer 4 Sagging at a support
At the end the wind relieves, the beam-end moment is M_w − M_v; when the wind moment is the larger, the end sags: 2.28 kN m at A of frame ABCD by the course method. The section then needs bottom bars carried into the support and anchored there, not stopped short as for a hogging end. On the EN 1990 route the check is 1.0G_k + 1.5W_k, which finds much larger reversals.

[glossary-lateral-load] Glossary: lateral load
lateral load: A horizontal action on the frame: the wind (Unit 5) and, by EC2, the equivalent forces of the geometric imperfections.

[glossary-sway] Glossary: sway
sway: The sideways movement of the floors of an unbraced frame under lateral load; each storey drifts relative to the one below.

[glossary-double-curvature] Glossary: double curvature
double curvature: A member bent by end moments that turn the same way, as a column of a swaying storey: the moment changes sign between the ends.

[glossary-point-of-contraflexure] Glossary: point of contraflexure
point of contraflexure: Where the bending moment changes sign. Both approximate methods put one at the mid-height of every column and the mid-span of every beam.

[glossary-storey-shear-v] Glossary: storey shear V
storey shear V: The sum of the lateral forces above a cut through a storey; the column shears of the storey add up to it.

[glossary-overturning-moment-m-o] Glossary: overturning moment M_o
overturning moment M_o: The moment of the lateral forces above the cut, about the cut at the mid-height of the storey: ΣF(z − z_{cut} ).

[glossary-cantilever-method] Glossary: cantilever method
cantilever method: The frame bends as one cantilever about the centroid of its columns: column axial forces in proportion to their distance from the centroid (equal areas). Suits tall, slender frames.

[glossary-portal-method] Glossary: portal method
portal method: Each bay acts as a portal: the storey shear is shared by the bays in proportion to their spans, half to each leg. Suits low, wide frames.

[glossary-centroid-x] Glossary: centroid x
centroid x: Σx_i A_i /ΣA_i of the columns of a storey; with equal areas, the average column position.

[glossary-r-i-p] Glossary: r_i , P
r_i , P: r_i = d_i /d_{min} , the column’s distance from the centroid over the smallest one; P = M_o /Σ|r||d|, the axial force at d_{min} ; N_i = r_i P.

[glossary-column-shear-h] Glossary: column shear H
column shear H: The horizontal force in a column at its point of contraflexure; M_{col} = H h/2 at each end.

[glossary-beam-shear-f] Glossary: beam shear F
beam shear F: The vertical force in a beam at its mid-span: the change of axial force to the left (cantilever) or 2M_b /L (portal); M_{beam} = F L/2.

[glossary-k-i] Glossary: k_i
k_i: The portal share of column i, (L_{left} + L_{right} )/(2ΣL); H_i = k_i V.

[glossary-joint-balance] Glossary: joint balance
joint balance: At a joint the beam moments balance the column moments: M_{b,right} = M_{c,above} + M_{c,below} − M_{b,left} , joint by joint from the windward side.

[glossary-bs-8110-load-combination-3] Glossary: BS 8110 load combination 3
BS 8110 load combination 3: Dead, imposed and wind together at 1.2(G_k + Q_k + W_k ): the course method, with every span loaded.

[glossary-moment-reversal] Glossary: moment reversal
moment reversal: A beam end whose hogging moment the wind turns into sagging, when M_w > M_v ; it needs bottom steel at the support, anchored into the column.

[glossary-en-1990-eq-6-10] Glossary: EN 1990 Eq. 6.10
EN 1990 Eq. 6.10: The fundamental combination: one leading variable action at 1.5, the others at 1.5ψ_0 ; G at 1.35, or 1.0 where it helps.

[glossary-0] Glossary: ψ_0
ψ_0: The combination factor of an accompanying variable action; the app takes 0.7 for the imposed load and 0.5 for the wind.

[glossary-stiffness-analysis] Glossary: stiffness analysis
stiffness analysis: A full analysis of the frame (the stiffness method in a computer program), which finds the points of contraflexure from the member stiffnesses; the approximate methods check its order of magnitude.

[glossary-professional-habit-6] Glossary: Professional Habit 6
Professional Habit 6: Check every storey’s equilibrium before using its moments: ΣH = V and, for the cantilever method, ΣN_i x_i about the centroid = M_o .
